headline: 550,000 students drop out of HSC exams this year
summary: More than one in three expected candidates vanished before the exam hall, signaling a silent crisis in the education system.
details: Around 550,000 students who registered for Class XI did not submit forms for the HSC and equivalent examinations this year. Additionally, 24,784 candidates were absent on the first day of the exams.

Possible reasons for this massive dropout rate include failing internal selection tests, fear of strict invigilation policies, and the rising cost of education making it unaffordable for many families.

Some students may have migrated or are preparing to migrate, while some girls were married off. Many families now view education as a poor investment due to high ancillary costs and uncertain job prospects.
The author argues that colleges often use internal tests as a 'trapdoor' to remove weak students to maintain institutional statistics rather than providing the necessary academic support.

This trend is alarming as HSC-level education is critical for upward mobility. Without these skills, dropouts entering the workforce or agriculture are likely to remain trapped in low-wage, low-skill jobs.
The crisis highlights a systemic failure where the HSC exam has become a checkpoint rather than a bridge to higher education and professional growth.
caption:
Over 550,000 students vanished from the HSC exam process this year. Why are they leaving?

Around 550,000 students who registered for Class XI did not submit forms for the HSC and equivalent examinations this year. Additionally, 24,784 candidates were absent on the first day of the exams.

The author argues that colleges often use internal tests as a 'trapdoor' to remove weak students to maintain institutional statistics rather than providing the necessary academic support.

This trend is alarming as HSC-level education is critical for upward mobility. Without these skills, dropouts entering the workforce or agriculture are likely to remain trapped in low-wage, low-skill jobs.

The crisis highlights a systemic failure where the HSC exam has become a checkpoint rather than a bridge to higher education and professional growth.

headline_marked: 55% of government schools [[lack a headteacher]], teacher shortage persists
headline: 55% of government schools lack a headteacher, teacher shortage persists
summary: Over half of the country's government secondary schools are operating without a headteacher, while thousands of teaching positions remain vacant.
details: Across 702 government secondary schools in Bangladesh, 383 headteacher positions are vacant, meaning roughly 55% of these institutions are without a permanent head.

The crisis extends to other staff; 2,842 assistant teacher positions are empty, representing over 18% of the total approved posts. This leaves many schools struggling to maintain basic educational standards.
At Shahid Manu Mia Government High School in Dhaka, only 9 teachers serve 420 students, resulting in a ratio of 47 students per teacher—far exceeding the recommended 30:1 ratio.
The shortage is severe enough that headteachers and assistant headteachers are forced to take regular classes, with some teachers taking five to six classes per day.
Administrative gaps are also widespread. All 16 school inspector positions are vacant, and 23 out of 64 district education officers' posts are empty, causing a stagnation in oversight and management.
Critics argue that the government has focused more on infrastructure, such as building new classrooms, than on recruiting the necessary human resources to actually teach the students.
The Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE) stated they are working with the Public Service Commission (PSC) to fill these vacancies and resolve promotion-related complexities.
caption:
Over half of Bangladesh's government secondary schools have no headteacher. How can quality education be ensured?

Across 702 government secondary schools in Bangladesh, 383 headteacher positions are vacant, meaning roughly 55% of these institutions are without a permanent head.

The crisis extends to other staff; 2,842 assistant teacher positions are empty, representing over 18% of the total approved posts. This leaves many schools struggling to maintain basic educational standards.

At Shahid Manu Mia Government High School in Dhaka, only 9 teachers serve 420 students, resulting in a ratio of 47 students per teacher—far exceeding the recommended 30:1 ratio.

The shortage is severe enough that headteachers and assistant headteachers are forced to take regular classes, with some teachers taking five to six classes per day.

Administrative gaps are also widespread. All 16 school inspector positions are vacant, and 23 out of 64 district education officers' posts are empty, causing a stagnation in oversight and management.

Critics argue that the government has focused more on infrastructure, such as building new classrooms, than on recruiting the necessary human resources to actually teach the students.

The Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE) stated they are working with the Public Service Commission (PSC) to fill these vacancies and resolve promotion-related complexities.
